task_title: Change of Airspeed in Straight-and-Level and Turning Flight
area: Area VI. Flight by Reference to Instruments
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain why the bank must change with airspeed to hold a standard-rate turn, teach how to hold altitude while changing airspeed in straight-and-level and turning flight on round dials and glass, full panel and partial panel, coach the power, pitch, rudder and trim that go with every speed change, fly it from the right seat while explaining it, and analyze and correct the common errors an examiner simulates.
why: The IFH calls airspeed changes in straight-and-level flight an excellent way to build all three basic instrument skills, and says they bring out the common errors of training [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]; in turns, every component of control changes at once [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. Real IFR flying needs the skill: ATC issues speed adjustments for spacing [[33:282|AIM 4-4-12]], and pilots must understand how the bank varies with speed changes, such as slowing down for holding or an instrument approach [[23:88|IFH 4-11]]. The IFH racetrack and circling approach practice patterns both begin with this kind of speed change [[23:191|IFH 7-30]] [[23:193|IFH 7-32]].

warmup: Think first: your student holds a perfect standard-rate turn at 120 knots, then pulls the power back to slow to 90 knots for an approach. She keeps the same bank and the same nose attitude. What will the turn coordinator, the altimeter and the airspeed do over the next 20 seconds, and which one will she notice first?

chunks.title: What this Task adds, and how it is tested

body.p: **Teaching change of airspeed in straight-and-level flight and turns** builds directly on Task A. The lesson FII.VI.A already covers the two methods, the instrument groups, how to recognize and simulate failures, the positive exchange of controls and the general straight-and-level error lists, so this lesson does not repeat them. Here the focus is what happens when the speed changes: pitch, bank, power and trim all have to move together.

The IFH calls airspeed changes in straight-and-level flight an excellent way to develop all three basic instrument skills, and says they bring out common errors to expect in training [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]. Changing airspeed in turns goes further: the maneuver changes all components of control at once, so it needs a rapid cross-check, sharp interpretation and smooth control [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

It is also everyday IFR flying. ATC issues speed adjustments to radar-controlled aircraft for spacing [[33:282|AIM 4-4-12]]; a pilot 3 minutes or less from a clearance limit with no further clearance starts slowing to cross the fix at or below the maximum holding airspeed [[33:382|AIM 5-3-8]]; and the IFH ties the bank-speed relationship to slowing down for holding or an approach [[23:88|IFH 4-11]].

chunks.title: Why the bank must change with airspeed

body.p: **Standard rate is a rate, not a bank angle.** A standard-rate turn is 3° per second, a full circle in 2 minutes, and it takes more bank as airspeed increases [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. Rate of turn comes from a set bank at a set speed: change either one and the rate changes [[23:88|IFH 4-11]].

The reason: in a bank, lift splits into a vertical part that holds the airplane up and a horizontal part that pulls it around the turn; at any given airspeed, the horizontal part grows with the bank [[1:119|PHAK 5-22]] [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]]. The PHAK formula puts numbers on it: rate of turn = 1,091 × tangent of the bank ÷ true airspeed in knots [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]] [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]]. Speed is under the line, so at the same bank a slower airplane turns faster and a faster one turns slower [[23:88|IFH 4-11]].

body.p: **The IFH procedure follows from it.** Since the turns are flown at standard rate, the bank must be varied in direct proportion to the airspeed change to keep the rate constant [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. During a reduction of airspeed, decrease the bank and increase the pitch attitude to hold altitude and a standard-rate turn [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. Speeding up is the reverse: hold the rate by increasing the bank [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]].

Two linked facts close the loop. Turning costs vertical lift, so the nose must come up a little as the bank goes in [[23:181|IFH 7-20]], and the added angle of attack adds induced drag, so power is needed to hold speed in a level turn [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]]. Slowing in the turn adds a second reason to raise the nose: a slower airplane needs a higher pitch attitude to stay level [[23:172|IFH 7-11]].

callout.text: Application: teach it with the instrument, not the formula. Have the student hold the turn coordinator on the standard-rate mark while you move the throttle. She will see the bank shallow as the speed falls and steepen as it builds, because the IFH tells her to adjust the bank whenever the miniature airplane leaves the desired deflection [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

check.q: Your student slows from 120 to 100 knots in a standard-rate turn but holds 18° of bank. What happens, and what bank does she need?
check.a: At the lower speed the same bank gives a faster turn, so the turn coordinator moves past the standard-rate mark [[23:88|IFH 4-11]]. By the rule of thumb she needs about 15° at 100 knots [[23:181|IFH 7-20]], and she must raise the pitch to hold altitude [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

chunks.title: Power, pitch and trim: why they move together

body.p: **Coordination of controls and trim technique** starts with what each control does during a speed change. For changes in airspeed in straight-and-level flight, pitch, bank and power must be coordinated to hold altitude and heading [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]. A single-engine propeller airplane tends to change attitude around all axes when the power changes, so control pressures are applied in proportion to the power change [[23:170|IFH 7-9]].

body.p: Power and pitch split the work. At any given airspeed the power decides whether the airplane is level, climbing or descending; with altitude held constant, the power decides the airspeed [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]. So in a speed change at constant altitude the throttle sets the new speed and the elevator holds the altitude. Control feel changes too: a changing airspeed changes the effectiveness of a given control pressure, so keep cross-checking as you relax pressures [[23:165|IFH 7-4]].

Trim ties it together. Trim tabs work on airflow, so trim is a function of speed: any change in speed needs a retrim, and an airplane trimmed in pitch seeks to return to the speed it was trimmed for [[23:85|IFH 4-8]]. That is why the IFH says an airplane is trimmed for an airspeed, not a pitch attitude or altitude, and that the airspeed must be held constant before the final trim [[23:204|IFH 7-43]].

callout.text: Throttle for speed, elevator for altitude, rudder for the ball, trim for the pressure. In a turn, the bank follows the speed.

check.q: After slowing from 120 to 100 knots your student holds back pressure but never retrims. She lets go to copy a clearance. What happens?
check.a: The airplane is still trimmed for 120 knots and seeks to return to that speed [[23:85|IFH 4-8]], so the nose drops and she loses altitude. Trim sets an airspeed: retrim after every speed change [[23:204|IFH 7-43]].

chunks.title: Full panel, straight-and-level: the IFH slowdown

body.p: **Procedure using full panel for maintaining altitude and changing airspeed in straight-and-level flight.** Power changes are much easier when the approximate power settings for each airspeed are known in advance [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]. To change airspeed by any appreciable amount, underpower or overpower on the first power change to speed up the change; for small changes, or airplanes that slow down or speed up quickly, this is not needed [[23:170|IFH 7-9]].
The IFH example airplane needs 23 inches of manifold pressure for 120 knots and 18 inches for 100 knots [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]. In primary-and-supporting words:

body.p: With practice, the power is set with only a brief glance at the gauge, by feeling the throttle move, hearing the change in sound and feeling the control pressures change [[23:170|IFH 7-9]] [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]. As proficiency comes, the student controls the change with no deviation of heading or altitude [[23:172|IFH 7-11]].

**Speeding up** is the mirror image: overpower, hold forward pressure as the speed builds so the airplane does not climb, and counter the yaw and roll to the left [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]. Bring the power back to the new setting before the target; as in a level-off at cruise, the lead depends on how fast the airplane accelerates [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

In control-and-performance words the same change is: set the new power on the power instruments and the new attitude on the attitude indicator, trim, cross-check altimeter, airspeed and VSI, then adjust [[23:135|IFH 6-2]] [[23:136|IFH 6-3]]. At a constant airspeed there is only one pitch attitude for level flight, nose-higher at slower speeds [[23:163|IFH 7-2]], so the slow-speed picture is a new attitude to learn, not an error.

callout.text: Analog attitude indicators may show a slight nose-up error in a rapid acceleration and a nose-down error in a rapid deceleration; the errors are small and correct themselves within a minute or so [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]. Application: one more reason to watch the altimeter and VSI, not the attitude picture alone, while the speed changes.

check.q: Your student sets 18 inches at once for the 120 to 100 knot change, and the airplane takes a long time to slow. What technique speeds it up?
check.a: Underpower: smoothly to about 15 inches, then set about 18 inches as the speed nears 100 knots [[23:170|IFH 7-9]] [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]. For small changes, or airplanes that slow quickly, it is not needed [[23:170|IFH 7-9]].

chunks.title: Adding gear and flaps to the slowdown

body.p: Once the student can change speed clean, the IFH adds speed changes while extending or retracting the flaps and gear, always within the POH/AFM gear and flap speed limits [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]. Some airplanes need sudden, exaggerated attitude changes: the nose tends to pitch down when the gear goes down, and flaps add lift for a moment at partial settings, then a marked increase in drag near full extension [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]. Knowing the power settings and trim changes for each mix of speed, gear and flaps cuts cross-check and interpretation problems [[23:172|IFH 7-11]].

The IFH example: clean, 120 knots at 23 inches and 2,300 rpm; with gear and flaps down, level flight at the same altitude needs 25 inches and 2,500 rpm; gear limit 115 knots, flap limit 105 knots; target 95 knots [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]. The steps:

bullets: 1. Maintain 2,500 rpm (the clean cruise example used 2,300), since a high power setting is used in the full drag configuration [[23:172|IFH 7-11]] [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].
2. Reduce manifold pressure to 10 inches; as the airspeed decreases, speed up the cross-check [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].
3. Trim for the increased angle of attack and the decrease in torque [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].
4. Lower the gear at 115 knots. The nose may pitch down and the airplane slows faster: raise the pitch to hold altitude and trim off some of the back pressure [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

5. Since 18 inches holds 100 knots with the gear down, set it smoothly as the airspeed reaches about 105 knots. The attitude indicator now shows about two-and-a-half bar widths nose-high in level flight [[23:173|IFH 7-12]] [[23:203|IFH 7-42]].

6. Lower the flaps and at the same time add power to 25 inches; trim off the pressures that hold altitude and heading. At 95 knots, level, the attitude indicator shows about one bar width nose-low [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

body.p: If full flaps go down at 105 knots, cross-check, interpretation and control must be very rapid; the simpler technique is to stabilize the attitude with the gear down before lowering the flaps [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]. Proficiency means a constant altitude and heading with smooth pitch, bank, power and trim control through these pronounced attitude changes [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

callout.text: Application: in a fixed-gear trainer, fly the same drill with flaps only, using the POH flap speed and the power that holds level flight in each configuration. Have the student write the numbers on a card before the flight.

check.q: Your student lowers the gear at 115 knots and loses 70 feet as the nose drops. What did she miss?
check.a: The nose tends to pitch down when the gear extends and the airplane slows faster; she must raise the pitch to hold altitude and trim off some back pressure [[23:172|IFH 7-11]] [[23:173|IFH 7-12]], with a faster cross-check as the speed falls [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

chunks.title: Full panel turns: changing airspeed at standard rate

body.p: **Procedure using full panel for maintaining altitude and changing airspeed in turning flight.** Pitch and power technique is the same as for airspeed changes in straight-and-level flight [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. What is new is the bank. The altimeter and the turn coordinator should read the same all the way through [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

body.p: **Two methods** may be used. In the first, the turn is established and then the airspeed is changed. In the second, the speed change starts with the turn entry. The first is easier, but either way the cross-check must speed up as the power is reduced [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. Until control is very smooth, check the attitude indicator often, to prevent overcontrolling and to give approximate bank angles for the changing airspeeds [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

Roll-in and roll-out rules still apply. Set the approximate bank on the attitude indicator, then use the turn coordinator as the primary bank reference with the attitude indicator supporting; if the speed is to stay constant, the airspeed indicator is primary for power and the throttle is adjusted as drag increases [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Pitch, bank and airspeed errors feed each other in turns, so the cross-check must be fast to keep errors from piling up [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

callout.text: Application: before and after the change, have the student read the bank on the attitude indicator's scale at standard rate, as the IFH suggests for any standard-rate turn [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Seeing 18° become 15° makes the idea stick.

check.q: Which method would you teach first for a speed change in a turn, and why?
check.a: The first: establish the turn, then change the speed. The IFH calls it easier; either way the cross-check must speed up as the power comes off [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. Add the simultaneous entry once the first is smooth, simple to complex [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

body.p: **Procedure using full panel on an electronic flight display.** The IFH flies the same 120 to 100 knot slowdown on a PFD with the same primaries: altimeter for pitch, heading indicator for bank, airspeed for power. The manifold pressure gauge is momentarily primary at the 15 inch underpower setting, and the airspeed is primary again once about 18 inches is set near 100 knots [[23:201|IFH 7-40]].

body.p: The glass section of the IFH has no separate text on changing airspeed in turns. Application: fly the round-dial procedure with the glass instruments, holding the turn rate trend vector on the standard-rate mark and shallowing the bank as the speed falls [[23:185|IFH 7-24]] [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].

callout.text: Fixation is a major error on glass: students put all their attention on the turn rate indicator and abandon the cross-check. A modified radial scan helps [[23:213|IFH 7-52]].

check.q: On a PFD your student slows in a standard-rate turn. Which instrument tells her to change the bank, and what does it show?
check.a: The turn rate indicator, primary for bank in a standard-rate turn [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]. As the speed falls at a constant bank, the rate increases [[23:88|IFH 4-11]], so the trend vector grows past the standard-rate mark [[23:160|IFH 6-27]] until she shallows the bank.

chunks.title: Partial panel: speed changes without the gyros

body.p: **Procedure using partial panel for maintaining altitude and changing airspeed.** Except the instrument takeoff, every IFH maneuver can be flown with the attitude gyro and heading indicator covered or inoperative [[23:162|IFH 7-1]], and on glass with the AHRS simulated or inoperative [[23:194|IFH 7-33]]. The PTS requires you to teach Area VI both ways [[FAA-S-8081-9E:17|PTS Emphasis on Attitude Instrument Flying and Partial Panel Skills]].

body.p: **The compass and speed changes.** On an east or west heading, acceleration gives a north-turn indication and deceleration a south-turn indication; on north or south headings, changing airspeed causes no error [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. Abrupt changes in attitude or airspeed make the card swing and very hard to read [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. Teach the student to hold the turn coordinator level during a straight slowdown and to read the compass only in straight, unaccelerated flight [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

**The transition is the hard part.** Without the attitude indicator, the IFH warns that in a descent the airspeed, altimeter and VSI show varying rates until the airplane settles at a constant speed and attitude, so control pressures, trim and cross-check must be accurate through the transition [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]; a partial panel speed change has the same kind of transition (Application). Keep inputs small and smooth: abrupt reactions to altitude changes set up an oscillation that can disorient the pilot and fix her on the altimeter, costing directional and airspeed control [[23:197|IFH 7-36]]. Rolling out at the same rate as the roll-in makes the roll-out lead easier to judge, especially partial panel [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

**Glass partial panel.** In the IFH example an AHRS failure removes all attitude and heading indications from the PFD [[23:217|IFH 7-56]], and the standby group is an analog airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and compass, with no standby turn coordinator [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. Application: with no rate instrument left, set the standard-rate bank on the standby attitude indicator from the rule of thumb for the present true airspeed [[23:180|IFH 7-19]], shallow it as the airplane slows, and check the result with the clock and compass.

callout.text: Application: start partial panel speed changes on a north or south heading, where changing airspeed gives no compass error [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. Then repeat on east or west so the student sees the false turn and learns to leave it alone until the speed is steady.

check.q: Gyros covered, heading 270, your student slows from 120 to 100 knots and the compass swings toward south. She banks to correct it. What do you teach?
check.a: On a west heading, deceleration gives a south-turn indication [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. Hold the turn coordinator's airplane level with the ball centered [[23:168|IFH 7-7]] and read the compass only in straight, unaccelerated flight [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

chunks.title: Coordination of controls and trim technique

body.p: **Coordination of controls.** Any aileron use produces adverse yaw, so rudder is needed when entering and leaving turns, and the ball shows whether the turn is coordinated [[23:88|IFH 4-11]]. Ball off center toward the turn: the airplane is slipping, so add rudder on that side or reduce the bank. Ball off center away from the turn: it is skidding, so relax rudder toward the turn or increase the bank [[23:89|IFH 4-12]].

Power changes bring yaw of their own. With an increase in power the airplane tends to yaw and roll left [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]; as thrust decreases, be ready with left rudder, back pressure and aileron, because effective torque control means countering yaw with rudder pressure [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]. On a PFD, if the heading is steady but the roll pointer and roll index are not aligned, the airplane is uncoordinated: correct with rudder [[23:200|IFH 7-39]].

**Trim technique.** The order never changes: set the attitude with control pressure, then trim so the airplane holds it with the controls released; using trim alone to change attitude leads to erratic control [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]. Trim for coordinated flight with rudder trim toward the side the ball is displaced [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]. During a speed change:

bullets: Trim off the pressures as the airplane decelerates, not only at the end [[23:172|IFH 7-11]].
Make the final trim only once the airspeed is held constant; while it still changes, the trim cannot be set properly and the altitude varies [[23:204|IFH 7-43]].
Trim frequently and in small amounts; excessive trim creates pressures that must be held until the airplane is trimmed properly [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].
In turns, trim matters throughout the speed change [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]; check the ball all the way round, especially if pressures are held rather than trimmed off [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

callout.text: Application: teach the order out loud: "Throttle, pitch, rudder, then trim." Before the student touches the trim wheel, have her say which pressure she is holding. If she cannot say it, she is trimming by guess.

check.q: In a left standard-rate turn, after a power reduction, the ball is off center to the left. What is it, and what is the fix?
check.a: Ball toward the turn means a slip: add left rudder or reduce the bank [[23:89|IFH 4-12]], then trim with rudder trim toward the ball [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

chunks.title: Risk: illusions, slow speed and safe practice

body.p: Speed changes have their own disorientation risk. A rapid acceleration stimulates the otolith organs the way tilting the head back does, creating the somatogravic illusion of a nose-up attitude, and the disoriented pilot may push into a nose-low or dive attitude. A rapid deceleration from a quick throttle reduction can do the opposite, and the pilot may pull into a nose-up or stall attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. In IMC, large attitude changes risk loss of control and spatial disorientation [[23:205|IFH 7-44]]. So smooth throttle movement is a safety item, not only a technique item.

Long turns add another trap: in a prolonged constant-rate turn the inner ear stops sensing the turn, and the return to level can feel like a turn the other way [[23:72|IFH 3-5]]. Application: a long turn with a speed change is exactly that setup, so keep the student's eyes and trust on the instruments.

Slow speeds need care. In the region of reversed command the airplane tends to keep slowing, errors of technique are amplified and precise airspeed control matters [[23:85|IFH 4-8]]. Near the flat part of the drag curve a small power increase may not bring the speed back quickly, and more power than normal may be needed for a short time [[23:87|IFH 4-10]]. Stay within the POH/AFM gear and flap speed limits [[23:172|IFH 7-11]].

bullets: Lookout: simulated instrument flight needs a safety pilot in the other control seat [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]], and see and avoid applies whenever weather permits, IFR or VFR [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]]. Failure to clear the area before and while maneuvering is a typical reason for an unsatisfactory [[FAA-S-8081-9E:15|PTS Unsatisfactory Performance]].
Who flies: brief the positive three-step exchange of flight controls before the flight [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]; FII.VI.A has the full script.
Failures: simulate partial panel with covers, as the IFH describes [[23:162|IFH 7-1]]; FII.VI.A covers how to set up failures safely.
Errors you simulate: the PTS bars the examiner from simulating anything that may jeopardize safe flight [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]]. Hold yourself to the same rule.

callout.text: Learners should never be allowed to exceed the flight instructor's limits [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Application: before you let a student fly into an error, such as keeping the bank while slowing, brief a limit (a speed you will not go below, a bank you will not exceed) and take over at once if it is reached. Practice slow-speed changes with plenty of altitude below you.

check.q: To save time on a slowdown, your student snaps the throttle back in actual IMC. What risk do you point out?
check.a: A rapid deceleration from a quick throttle reduction can lead a disoriented pilot to pull into a nose-up or stall attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. Move the throttle smoothly to the underpower setting instead [[23:170|IFH 7-9]].

body.p: **Common errors related to changes of airspeed in straight-and-level and turning flight.** For S2 the examiner, acting as your student, flies these on purpose [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]]. For each: what you see, the usual cause, the fix and how you show it. FII.VI.A has the general straight-and-level lists; these are the ones a speed change brings out.
**Slow or improper cross-check during straight-and-level flight and turns.**

head: Error
What you see
Usual cause
Fix and how to teach it
rows: Scan not sped up
Altitude and heading drift as soon as the throttle moves
Failure to vary the rate of cross-check during speed, power or attitude changes [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]
Speed up the scan when the power changes; how much depends on the airplane, its torque and the size of the change [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]
Fixation on the power gauge
Eyes locked on manifold pressure or airspeed; altitude and heading wander, power and speed erratic
Unnecessary gazing at the power instrument during the change [[23:174|IFH 7-13]] [[23:206|IFH 7-45]]

A small power error matters less than large altitude and heading errors, and staring will not slow the airplane faster [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]. Teach setting power by feel and sound with a brief glance [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]
Heading left out
Heading creeps off during the power change
Failure to cross-check the heading indicator, especially during power or pitch changes [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Heading in every pass; counter yaw with rudder [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]
Bank crowds out pitch
Altitude lost while rolling in and slowing
Preoccupation with bank control during turn entry [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Check pitch as the bank pressures start; control the total attitude, not one factor at a time [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Airspeed left out
Speed overshoots the new value in the turn
Failure to cross-check the airspeed indicator as pitch changes are made [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Airspeed in each pass while the pitch is changing [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Glass fixation
Stare at the turn rate indicator or the 1-knot airspeed tape
All attention on one display [[23:213|IFH 7-52]] [[23:161|IFH 6-28]]
Modified radial scan [[23:213|IFH 7-52]]
Compass chased (partial panel)
Bank corrections for a compass swing during the speed change
Reading the compass before straight, unaccelerated flight; on east or west headings speed changes show false turns [[23:183|IFH 7-22]] [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Turn coordinator level, ball centered; read the compass once steady [[23:168|IFH 7-7]] [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]

body.p: **Improper power control.**

head: Error
What you see
Usual cause
Fix and how to teach it
rows: Settings unknown
Power hunting after every change
Failure to know the power settings and pitch attitudes for each airspeed and configuration [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Brief the POH numbers; known settings make speed changes much easier [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]
Abrupt throttle
Pitch and yaw jumps; illusion risk in IMC
Abrupt use of the throttle [[23:174|IFH 7-13]] [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]
Smooth throttle to the underpower setting [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]
Failure to lead the airspeed
Speed undershoots the target, then more power changes
New power set only when the target is reached [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Set the new power before the target; the lead depends on how fast the airplane responds [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Erratic power in turns
Speed and power chase each other
Throttle friction, inaccurate settings, chasing the airspeed, abrupt pitch and bank changes, or no recheck after a power change [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Set the friction, set a number, then recheck the airspeed [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Throttle not coordinated with the turn
Speed sags on roll-in and builds on roll-out
Slow cross-check or not understanding the aerodynamics of turns [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Add power as drag increases in the turn [[23:181|IFH 7-20]] [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]]

body.p: **How to show them** (Application):

bullets: Fixation: fly one slowdown while staring at the manifold pressure gauge, then ask the student what the altimeter and heading did. Then fly it again with a brief glance and a normal scan.
Slow scan: have the student call out each instrument as she looks at it during a slowdown. If the calls slow down when the throttle moves, she has found the error herself.
Underpower: fly the 120 to 100 knot change twice, once with the power set straight to the new value and once with underpower, and compare the time each takes [[23:170|IFH 7-9]].
Leading: leave the power at the underpower setting until the target on purpose, and let the student watch the speed sag below it [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].

check.q: As the examiner slows in a turn, he keeps his eyes on the manifold pressure gauge and drifts 120 feet high. What do you say?
check.a: Name it: fixation on the power instrument during an airspeed change. Cause: staring will not slow the airplane faster, and a small power error matters less than a large altitude error [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]. Fix: set the power with a brief glance and feel [[23:170|IFH 7-9]], back to the scan, and a small pitch correction.

chunks.title: Common errors: corrections, coordination and trim

body.p: **Failure to make smooth, precise corrections, as required.**

head: Error
What you see
Usual cause
Fix and how to teach it
rows: Bank not varied with speed
Turn coordinator or turn rate trend past the standard-rate mark as the speed falls, short of it as the speed builds
Bank held while the airspeed changes; at a constant bank the rate changes with speed [[23:88|IFH 4-11]]
Less bank as you slow, more as you speed up [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]
Pitch not varied with speed
Altitude lost while slowing, gained while speeding up
No proportionate pitch increase as the speed falls [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]; no forward pressure as it builds [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]
Cross-check the altimeter and VSI as the airplane decelerates [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]
Overcontrolling
Overbanking on entry, heading overshoots, pitch, airspeed and trim errors made worse
Large, quick inputs [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Check the attitude indicator often until control is smooth [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Pitch changed too soon
Nose comes up before the bank does, then swings
Mechanical, early back pressure with a slow cross-check and a fast entry [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Roll in no faster than the scan can follow [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]
Altitude gained on roll-out
Climbs on every roll-out
Pitch not adjusted as the vertical lift returns [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Lower the pitch as the bank comes off [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]
Rushed pitch correction
A large pitch change makes the error worse
Hurrying the correction [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]
Small corrections; FII.VI.A gives the sizes [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]

body.p: **Uncoordinated use of controls.**

head: Error
What you see
Usual cause
Fix and how to teach it
rows: Torque not countered
Heading swings and the ball moves with each power change
No rudder and aileron with the power change [[23:170|IFH 7-9]] [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]
Rudder with the throttle and a faster scan [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]
Ball ignored in the turn
Turn coordinator on the mark, ball off center
Failure to check the ball when reading the turn coordinator for bank [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Unless the ball is centered, do not assume the turn comes from bank [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]; fix with rudder or bank [[23:89|IFH 4-12]]
Rudder used for rate
Turn coordinator pushed to the mark with rudder; ball out
A pedal input shows a turn on the turn coordinator with no bank [[23:168|IFH 7-7]]
Rate comes from bank: coordinated aileron and rudder [[23:88|IFH 4-11]]
Heading overcontrolled
Back-and-forth heading corrections while the power moves
Overcontrolling heading changes during power changes; early rudder [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Small coordinated corrections with very light pressure [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]

body.p: **Improper trim technique.**

head: Error
What you see
Usual cause
Fix and how to teach it
rows: No trim after power changes
Pressures build; the nose wanders during a distraction
Failure to trim following power changes [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Trim off pressures as the speed changes [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]
Final trim too early
Retrimming while the speed still changes; altitude wanders
Not knowing trim sets an airspeed [[23:204|IFH 7-43]]
Hold the speed constant, then the final trim [[23:204|IFH 7-43]]
No trim in the turn
Tension on the controls
Failure to trim during entry and after a prolonged turn [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]; entry too fast for the scan [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Slower entry; trim throughout [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Chasing the VSI
Constant pitch changes; nothing gets trimmed
Overcontrolling causes tension and hides the pressures to trim off [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Hold a pitch and cross-check the other pitch instruments [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]
Trim used to fly
Attitude changed with the trim wheel; erratic control
Not understanding trim and its relation to attitude and power [[23:187|IFH 7-26]] [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]
Pressure first, then trim [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]

body.p: **How to show them** (Application):

bullets: Bank with speed: in a standard-rate turn, hold the bank on purpose while you slow and let the student watch the turn coordinator go past the mark [[23:88|IFH 4-11]]; then repeat, shallowing the bank to keep it on the mark [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].
Coordination: add power briskly with your feet flat and let the student see the heading and ball move, then repeat with rudder [[23:170|IFH 7-9]].
Rudder for rate: push rudder alone in a turn and show the turn coordinator move with the ball out [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].
Trim: slow to 100 knots without retrimming, then relax the back pressure with the student watching the nose drop and the speed build toward the old trim speed [[23:85|IFH 4-8]].

check.q: The examiner, as student, speeds up from 90 to 120 knots in a right standard-rate turn and pushes right rudder to bring the turn coordinator back to the mark. Name the error and the fix.
check.a: Uncoordinated use of controls: rudder alone shows a turn on the turn coordinator [[23:168|IFH 7-7]] and leaves the ball out [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]. At the higher speed the same bank gives less rate [[23:88|IFH 4-11]], so add bank with coordinated aileron and rudder [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

chunks.title: Teaching it: building blocks and the IFH pattern drills

body.p: When more than one skill is taught at a time, the simple-to-complex strategy works well; when the new skill builds on ones already learned, known to unknown helps [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Speed changes build on straight-and-level flight and turns. A sequence that follows the IFH (the order is Application):

head: Step
What the student practices
Source
rows: 1. Level, clean
Small and large speed changes, underpower and overpower, primaries, trim
2. Level, configuration
Speed changes with gear and flaps, within limits
3. Turning, easier method
Speed change after the turn is established
4. Turning, harder method
Speed change starting with the turn entry
5. Patterns
Combinations that simulate holding, procedure turns and approaches, once basic maneuvers are reasonably good
6. Partial panel
Steps 1 to 5 with the gyros covered or the AHRS simulated

body.p: **The racetrack pattern** is the IFH's classic speed-change drill, flown entirely in level flight: 3 minutes straight from A to B while slowing to holding speed; a 180° standard-rate turn to the right; 1 minute straight; another 180° right; then 1 minute on the original heading, adjusting the outbound leg so the inbound segment is 1 minute [[23:191|IFH 7-30]]. It combines the clock with basic maneuvers [[23:191|IFH 7-30]], and it mirrors real holding, where the pilot starts slowing 3 minutes or less from the clearance limit [[33:382|AIM 5-3-8]].

**The circling approach patterns** add configuration: slow to approach speed on the first 2-minute leg, make a 45° standard-rate turn to the left, lower the gear and flaps on a later straight leg, turn right 180°, then descend 500 feet at 500 fpm and go into a straight constant-airspeed climb while retracting the gear and flaps [[23:193|IFH 7-32]].

callout.text: Application: once the patterns go well in the same order, mix them up. Random practice gives better long-term retention than repeating one drill [[25:78|AIH 3-27]], and a student who flies a maneuver well but may not understand it should vary it or combine it with others [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

check.q: Your student flies the racetrack well but always reaches B still slowing. What do you change?
check.a: Start the power reduction at A with an underpower setting [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]; the pattern gives her the whole 3-minute leg from A to B for the slowdown [[23:191|IFH 7-30]], just as a pilot starts slowing 3 minutes or less from a holding fix [[33:382|AIM 5-3-8]].

body.p: In the telling-and-doing technique you **demonstrate and simultaneously explain**: fly the maneuver while explaining the power settings and attitudes, in the same order you briefed; if the demonstration strays from the explanation, say so at once. Next the student tells while you fly, so you can check her understanding before she is busy on the controls [[25:177|AIH 9-7]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. The PTS expects the explanation to be clear, concise, technically accurate and complete with no prompting [[FAA-S-8081-9E:15|PTS Unsatisfactory Performance]].
**Level slowdown, primary-and-supporting words** (IFH example airplane):

bullets: "Level at 120 knots, 23 inches. Altimeter primary for pitch, heading indicator for bank, airspeed for power [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]."
"Throttle smoothly back to about 15 inches to underpower. The manifold pressure gauge is primary for power for the moment [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]."
"As we slow, I raise the nose a little at a time to hold altitude, hold a touch of left rudder for the torque change, and speed up my scan [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]."
"Trimming the back pressure off as we decelerate [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]."
"Nearing 100 knots: power to about 18 inches before we get there, so we don't undershoot. Airspeed is primary for power again [[23:172|IFH 7-11]] [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]."
"Steady at 100: final trim, hands off, cross-check altitude and heading [[23:204|IFH 7-43]]."

body.p: **Speed change in a standard-rate turn, first method:**

bullets: "Rolling right with coordinated aileron and rudder to about 18° for 120 knots, then the turn coordinator on the standard-rate mark [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]."
"Turn established. Altimeter primary for pitch, turn coordinator for bank [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]."
"Power to the underpower setting. Manifold pressure is primary while the speed changes, and my scan speeds up [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]."
"Speed falling, so the same bank would turn us faster. I shallow the bank to keep the turn coordinator on the mark and raise the nose to hold altitude [[23:88|IFH 4-11]] [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]."
"Ball centered, trimming as we go [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]."
"Near 100 knots, set the new power; airspeed primary for power. The bank is about 15° now [[23:185|IFH 7-24]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]."

body.p: **Partial panel version:** "Gyros covered. Pitch from the altimeter and VSI, since the airspeed is changing on purpose. Bank from the turn coordinator, ball centered. Compass only when we are steady: on this east heading, slowing will show a false turn to the south [[23:165|IFH 7-4]] [[23:168|IFH 7-7]] [[23:183|IFH 7-22]] [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]."

The same turn in control-and-performance words: "I set the new power on the manifold pressure gauge and a slightly higher, shallower attitude on the attitude indicator, trim, then cross-check the altimeter, airspeed and turn coordinator and adjust [[23:135|IFH 6-2]] [[23:136|IFH 6-3]] [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]."

callout.text: Application: rehearse these scripts aloud until you can keep talking through a correction without the numbers drifting. The PTS wants the maneuver flown to the instrument pilot skill level while you give effective instruction [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Flight Instructor Responsibility]].

check.q: During your demo the turn coordinator drifts past the mark as you slow, and you say nothing. What should you have done?
check.a: Acknowledge and explain the deviation at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]], then fix it in words the student can use: shallow the bank to hold standard rate as the speed falls [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

chunks.title: Analyze and correct: when the examiner flies the errors

body.p: For S2 you **analyze and correct simulated common errors**: the evaluator acts as a student during selected maneuvers so you can show you recognize, analyze and correct them [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]]. Use the same five steps every time: what you see, the name of the error, its cause, the fix, and a short demonstration if asked.

head: Examiner flies
You say
Source
rows: Holds 18° of bank while slowing to 100 knots; the turn coordinator goes past the mark
"We're turning faster than standard rate. Same bank, slower speed, faster turn. Shallow to about 15° and keep it on the mark."
Stares at the manifold pressure gauge; 100 feet high
"Fixation on the power gauge. A small power error matters less than the altitude. Set it with a glance, back to the scan, small pitch correction."
Leaves 15 inches in until 100 knots; the speed sags to 92
"Failure to lead the airspeed. Set 18 inches before reaching 100."
Adds power to speed up with no forward pressure; climbs 150 feet
"Power came in without forward pressure, so the pitch instruments show a climb. Forward pressure as the speed builds, then trim."
Final trim at 104 knots while still slowing
"Trimming for a speed you haven't reached. Trim off pressures as you go, final trim once the speed is steady."
Power change with no rudder; heading drifts 10°
"Torque not countered. Rudder with the throttle, and keep the heading in the scan."
Gyros covered, heading 090: banks to stop the compass swinging south as he slows
"That's deceleration error on an east heading, not a turn. Turn coordinator level, ball centered, read the compass when we're steady."

body.p: Correcting is not taking over at the first mistake. Safety permitting, let the student go part way into the error and find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]; if safety requires it, take the controls with the positive exchange [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Check understanding too: a student who flies the maneuver well but cannot vary it or combine it with another probably lacks the principles [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

callout.text: Application: the examiner may fly two errors at once, such as a held bank and a sinking altitude during a turning slowdown. Name the one that matters most for safety first, then the other, and give one fix at a time.

check.q: In a turning slowdown the examiner holds the bank and sinks 80 feet at the same time. What do you say first?
check.a: Both errors come from one cause: the speed changed and nothing else did. Name the bank first, since the rate is past standard and growing [[23:88|IFH 4-11]], then the pitch; the IFH fix covers both: decrease the bank and increase the pitch [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

scenario.title: Slowing for the hold: a turning speed change, full and partial panel
scenario.setup: You are a new CFII. Your instrument student, a private pilot, flies the school's retractable single, whose numbers match the IFH example: 23 inches holds 120 knots clean, 18 inches holds 100 knots, and the gear limit is 115 knots. Today's lesson is airspeed changes in level flight and in standard-rate turns, first full panel and then with the attitude and heading indicators covered, ending with the racetrack pattern. It is VMC with 5 miles in haze, in a practice area near a busy VOR, and you are the safety pilot.

questions.q: How do you sequence today's lesson, and why that order?
questions.a: Simple to complex and known to unknown [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]: level speed changes first, which build all three basic skills [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]; then the easier turning method, speed change after the turn is established, then the simultaneous one [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]; then the racetrack once the basic maneuvers are reasonably good [[23:191|IFH 7-30]]; partial panel last, with the gyros covered [[23:162|IFH 7-1]].

questions.q: In a standard-rate left turn at 120 knots she pulls the power to 15 inches. The turn coordinator moves past the mark and she is 80 feet low. Name what happened and give the fix.
questions.a: Two errors: the bank was held while slowing, so the rate of turn increased [[23:88|IFH 4-11]], and the pitch did not come up as the speed fell. During a reduction of airspeed, decrease the bank and increase the pitch to hold altitude and standard rate [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]: about 15° at 100 knots [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Fix the 80 feet with a small correction, about half a bar width [[23:165|IFH 7-4]].

questions.q: At 100 knots she is still holding back pressure and says her arm is tired. What do you coach?
questions.a: Trim off the pressures as the airplane decelerates, and make the final trim once the speed is constant [[23:172|IFH 7-11]] [[23:204|IFH 7-43]]. With the pressures relieved it is much easier to hold the attitude and attend to other duties [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]; unless the airplane is trimmed, she cannot tell whether a pressure change comes from aerodynamic changes or from her own movements [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

questions.q: You cover the gyros. On a heading of 090 she slows, the compass swings toward south, and she banks left to "fix" it. What do you say?
questions.a: Deceleration on an east heading gives a south-turn indication [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. Level the turn coordinator's airplane, center the ball [[23:168|IFH 7-7]], and read the compass only in straight, unaccelerated flight [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

questions.q: On the racetrack she reaches B still decelerating and rushes the turn. What do you change, and how does it tie to real IFR flying?
questions.a: Slow on the 3-minute A to B leg [[23:191|IFH 7-30]], using underpower to speed the change [[23:170|IFH 7-9]], and roll in no faster than her scan can follow [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. In real holding she starts slowing 3 minutes or less from the clearance limit [[33:382|AIM 5-3-8]].

questions.q: In the debrief she says, "The turns were fine." How do you assess the flight?
questions.a: Collaborative assessment: her self-assessment first, then a discussion comparing it with yours [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], judged element by element rather than on the overall result [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Name what went well, then the bank-with-speed and trim items to practice.

skills.do: From the right seat, fly a level slowdown with a configuration change and a speed change in a standard-rate turn, to the instrument pilot skill level, while explaining in your chosen method's words the primary instruments, why the bank changes with the speed, and the rudder and trim; then repeat with the gyros covered or the AHRS simulated.
skills.practice: Rehearse the scripts in the talk-through chunk aloud with a safety pilot [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]], demonstrating in the same order you explain and admitting any deviation at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

skills.do: When the examiner, acting as your student, flies a speed-change error, say what you see, name it, give its cause and the fix, and show the fix if asked; take the controls with the positive exchange if safety requires.
skills.practice: Take turns with another applicant flying the IFH error lists for speed changes and turns [[23:174|IFH 7-13]] [[23:186|IFH 7-25]] [[23:187|IFH 7-26]] in VMC, never simulating anything that could jeopardize safe flight [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]].

quiz.q: Your student asks why she must shallow the bank as she slows in a standard-rate turn. Which answer is right?
options: Lift drops at lower speed, so less bank is needed
The turn coordinator reads high when the speed falls
At a lower speed, the same bank gives a faster turn
Standard rate means a set bank of 15° at any speed
quiz.why: Rate of turn depends on bank and speed; slowing at the same bank increases the rate [[23:88|IFH 4-11]], so the IFH says to decrease the bank during a reduction of airspeed [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. Standard rate is 3° per second, and the bank it takes varies with true airspeed [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

quiz.q: Using the IFH rule of thumb, about what bank gives a standard-rate turn at 140 knots true airspeed?
options: About 21°
About 14°
About 30°
About 10.5°
quiz.why: 15 percent of TAS: 140 ÷ 10 = 14, plus half of 14 = 21° [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. 14° is only the first step of the rule.

quiz.q: Why does the IFH example pull the throttle to about 15 inches when 18 inches will hold the new 100 knots?
options: 15 inches is what holds 100 knots
It keeps the nose from rising as it slows
It cancels the left yaw from the engine
Underpowering speeds up the change
quiz.why: To change airspeed by any appreciable amount, the common procedure is to underpower or overpower on the first power change to speed up the change [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]. The example needs 18 inches for 100 knots, and the nose must actually come up as the speed drops [[23:170|IFH 7-9]] [[23:172|IFH 7-11]].

quiz.q: Your student will change airspeed in a standard-rate turn for the first time. Which IFH method do you teach first?
options: Start the speed change with the roll-in
Establish the turn, then change the speed
Change speed, then roll into the turn
Hold the bank and let the rate float
quiz.why: In the first method the airspeed is changed after the turn is established; in the second the change starts with the turn entry. The first is easier [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. Changing speed before rolling in is just a straight-and-level speed change.

quiz.q: Gyros covered, heading 090, your student slows from 120 to 100 knots and the compass shows a turn toward south. What do you tell her?
options: Deceleration error: hold the turn coordinator level
She is turning right: roll left to stop it
Use the heading indicator, not the compass
That is northerly turning error from her bank
quiz.why: On an east or west heading, deceleration gives a south-turn indication [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. Hold the turn coordinator's airplane level with the ball centered [[23:168|IFH 7-7]] and read the compass in straight, unaccelerated flight [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]. The heading indicator is covered in this exercise.

quiz.q: On a PFD, which instrument is primary for bank while your student changes speed in a standard-rate turn?
options: Attitude indicator roll scale
Heading indicator
Turn rate indicator
Slip/skid indicator
quiz.why: The turn rate indicator is the primary bank instrument in a standard-rate turn, the only instrument that shows standard rate; the attitude indicator sets the bank and supports [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]. The slip/skid indicator shows coordination, not rate [[23:199|IFH 7-38]].

quiz.q: Slowing from 120 to 100 knots, your student sets her final trim at 106 knots while the speed is still falling. What is the problem?
options: She should not trim at all while slowing
Final trim needs a steady airspeed first
Trim should be set before the power comes off
Rudder trim must always be set first
quiz.why: Trimming can be done in any transition, but before the final trim the airspeed must be held constant; otherwise the altitude varies until the trimmed speed is reached [[23:204|IFH 7-43]]. Trimming off pressures as the airplane decelerates is correct [[23:172|IFH 7-11]].

quiz.q: As the power comes back for a slowdown, which control pressures should your student be ready for?
options: Right rudder and forward pressure
Right rudder, back pressure, no aileron
Forward pressure only, no rudder
Left rudder, back pressure and aileron
quiz.why: As thrust decreases, be ready to apply left rudder, back-elevator and aileron pressure the instant the pitch and bank instruments show a deviation [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]. Right rudder and forward pressure go with adding power, which makes the airplane climb and yaw left [[23:170|IFH 7-9]].

quiz.q: In IMC your student snaps the throttle back to slow down quickly. What illusion risk does that create?
options: Feeling a turn the other way after a long turn
Pulling into a nose-up or stall attitude
Feeling a climb, then pushing the nose down
Feeling a bank and leaning in the seat
quiz.why: A rapid deceleration from a quick throttle reduction can make the disoriented pilot pull into a nose-up or stall attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. The nose-up illusion that leads to pushing over comes from rapid acceleration [[23:73|IFH 3-6]], and the false turn after a long turn is a different illusion [[23:72|IFH 3-5]].

quiz.q: Slowing to 95 knots with gear and flaps, what does the IFH call the simpler technique?
options: Lower gear and flaps together at 105 knots
Lower flaps first, then gear at 95 knots
Stabilize with the gear down before the flaps
Keep cruise power until the flaps are down
quiz.why: If full flaps are lowered at 105 knots, cross-check and control must be very rapid; a simpler technique is to stabilize attitude with the gear down before lowering the flaps [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]. In the example the gear limit is 115 knots and the flap limit 105 [[23:172|IFH 7-11]].

quiz.q: In the IFH racetrack pattern, where does the student slow to holding speed?
options: On the 3-minute leg from A to B
During the first 180° turn
On the 1-minute straight leg from C to D
After rolling out at the end
quiz.why: Step 1: time 3 minutes straight-and-level from A to B and reduce to holding speed during that interval; the turns at B and D are then flown at the new speed [[23:191|IFH 7-30]].

quiz.q: The examiner, as your student, slows in a standard-rate turn and loses 100 feet. Bank and power are right, but the nose stayed at the cruise attitude. What error do you name?
options: Failure to lead the airspeed
Overbanking on turn entry
Overcontrolling the pitch on the entry
Pitch not raised as the speed fell
quiz.why: As airspeed decreases, a proportionate increase in pitch is needed to hold altitude [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]; in a turn, decrease the bank and increase the pitch [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. Failure to lead the airspeed is a power error that shows up as a speed undershoot [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].

final_quiz.q: Your student speeds up from 90 to 120 knots in a coordinated standard-rate turn without changing the bank. What does the turn coordinator show?
options: Still exactly standard rate
Less than standard rate
More than standard rate
A skid, with the ball out
final_quiz.why: If speed increases without a change in bank, the rate of turn decreases [[23:88|IFH 4-11]], so she must add bank to hold standard rate [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]]. In coordinated flight the ball stays centered, so it is not a skid [[23:89|IFH 4-12]].

final_quiz.q: At 9,000 feet your student works out standard-rate bank from her indicated airspeed. What do you tell her?
options: Fine: indicated is what the rule uses
Use the GPS groundspeed instead
Use the 100-knot bank at every speed
Use true airspeed; the rule is built on TAS
final_quiz.why: The IFH rule of thumb is 15 percent of the true airspeed [[23:180|IFH 7-19]], and the PHAK's rate-of-turn math uses TAS [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]]. The turn coordinator then confirms standard rate [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

final_quiz.q: During a speed change in a standard-rate turn on round dials, which instrument is primary for pitch?
options: Attitude indicator
Vertical speed indicator
Altimeter
Airspeed indicator
final_quiz.why: The altimeter is primary for pitch and the turn coordinator's miniature airplane for bank; their indications should stay constant through the turn [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. Figure 7-38 labels the attitude indicator and VSI as supporting pitch [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

final_quiz.q: Your school's trainer has a fixed-pitch propeller. In the IFH slowdown, which gauge takes the place of the manifold pressure gauge?
options: Tachometer
Fuel flow gauge
Airspeed indicator
Suction gauge
final_quiz.why: The supporting power instrument is the manifold pressure gauge, or the tachometer if the propeller is fixed pitch [[23:170|IFH 7-9]].

final_quiz.q: To speed up from 100 to 120 knots at constant altitude, what must your student do with pitch as the power comes in?
options: Raise the nose to keep the speed in check
Nothing: the trim takes care of the pitch
Hold forward pressure as the speed builds
Lower the nose first, then add the power slowly
final_quiz.why: When power is added to increase airspeed, the pitch instruments show a climb unless forward pressure is applied as the airspeed changes [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]. Trim relieves pressure already held; it does not replace it [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

final_quiz.q: When should your student set the new, lower power during a slowdown?
options: Exactly when the target speed is reached
Before the target, by a lead that suits the airplane
Ten knots after the target, to let it settle
Only after the final trim is set
final_quiz.why: Adjust the throttle for the slower speed before the airspeed reaches it, or the airplane slows below the target and needs more power changes; the lead depends on how fast the airplane responds [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].

final_quiz.q: ATC asks your student for 10 knots slower in a light single that slows quickly. Does she need to underpower?
options: Yes: every speed change needs it
Yes: ATC expects it for spacing
No: underpowering is never used
No: small changes don't need it
final_quiz.why: For small speed changes, or in airplanes that slow down or speed up quickly, underpowering or overpowering is not necessary [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]. ATC gives speed adjustments in 5 or 10 knot steps [[33:283|AIM 4-4-12]].

final_quiz.q: ATC assigns your student 100 knots. Within what range is she expected to hold it?
options: Plus or minus 10 knots
Plus or minus 5 knots
Plus or minus 15 knots
Exactly 100 on the tape
final_quiz.why: Pilots complying with speed adjustments are expected to stay within plus or minus 10 knots or 0.02 Mach of the specified speed [[33:283|AIM 4-4-12]]. On glass, holding airspeed to 1 knot is unnecessary [[23:161|IFH 6-28]].

final_quiz.q: Nearing a clearance limit with no clearance beyond it, when is your student expected to start slowing?
options: Only once established in the hold
10 minutes before the fix
3 minutes or less from the fix
When ATC tells her to slow
final_quiz.why: When an aircraft is 3 minutes or less from a clearance limit and no clearance beyond the fix has been received, the pilot is expected to start a speed reduction to cross the fix at or below the maximum holding airspeed [[33:382|AIM 5-3-8]]. The racetrack's 3-minute leg rehearses it [[23:191|IFH 7-30]].

final_quiz.q: In the IFH glass example, the AHRS fails during a turning slowdown. What is left for bank?
options: The PFD turn rate indicator and trend
A standby turn coordinator below the MFD
The slip/skid indicator on the PFD
Standby attitude indicator; no turn coordinator
final_quiz.why: An AHRS failure removes all attitude and heading from the PFD, including the slip/skid indicator [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. The standby instruments are an analog airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and compass; the only turn coordinator sits behind the MFD for the autopilot, out of the pilot's reach [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].

final_quiz.q: Slowed to 100 knots with the gear down, the attitude indicator shows about two-and-a-half bar widths nose-high. Your student wants to reset the miniature airplane to show level. What do you say?
options: Reset it so that level flight looks level again
Leave it set at cruise so pitch reads true
Cage the gyro until the speed is steady
Reset it only once the flaps are down
final_quiz.why: Set the miniature aircraft in level flight at cruise; otherwise do not change it for other speeds, so the attitude indicator shows a true picture of pitch in all maneuvers [[23:138|IFH 6-5]]. The nose-high picture at slow speed is expected [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

final_quiz.q: Your student slows from 120 to 100 knots, never retrims, then lets go of the yoke to copy a clearance. What will the airplane try to do?
options: Nose down, back toward 120 knots
Hold 100 knots and the altitude
Pitch up and slow down toward a stall
Roll left from the lower torque
final_quiz.why: An airplane trimmed in pitch seeks to return to the speed it was trimmed for [[23:85|IFH 4-8]]. She is still trimmed for 120 knots, so the nose drops and the airplane speeds up. Any time the airspeed changes, retrim [[23:204|IFH 7-43]].

final_quiz.q: In a left standard-rate turn after a power change, the ball is off center to the right. What is it, and what fixes it?
options: A slip: add more left rudder pressure
A slip: reduce the angle of bank
A skid: add more left rudder pressure
A skid: ease rudder or add bank
final_quiz.why: Ball off center away from the turn means a skid: relax rudder toward the turn or increase the bank [[23:89|IFH 4-12]]. A ball toward the turn would be a slip, fixed with rudder on that side or less bank [[23:89|IFH 4-12]].

final_quiz.q: The examiner, as student, speeds up in a right standard-rate turn and pushes right rudder to bring the turn coordinator back to the mark. What do you say?
options: Good: rudder controls the rate of turn
Uncoordinated: add bank with aileron instead
Fine, as long as the altitude is held
Reduce power to slow the turn rate
final_quiz.why: A pedal input shows a turn on the turn coordinator without a bank [[23:168|IFH 7-7]], and unless the ball is centered the turn is not coming from bank [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]. At the higher speed the same bank gives less rate [[23:88|IFH 4-11]], so add bank with coordinated aileron and rudder [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

final_quiz.q: Your student flies the racetrack well, in the same order every lesson. How do you check that she understands it?
options: Have her vary it or combine it with others
Repeat the same drill until it is fully automatic
Grade it on altitude and heading tolerances only
Move on: flying it well proves she understands
final_quiz.why: A student who flies a maneuver well but may not understand it should vary it, combine it with other operations or apply its elements elsewhere; one who lacks the principles usually cannot [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Repeating one drill can fool both learner and instructor [[25:78|AIH 3-27]].

final_quiz.q: In circling approach pattern I, where does the student lower the gear and flaps?
options: On the 2-minute leg from A to B
In the 45° turn at B
On the 1-minute leg from C to D
During the 500 fpm descent after E
final_quiz.why: Slow to approach speed from A to B, turn 45° at B, fly 45 seconds to C, turn back to the original heading and fly 1 minute to D while lowering the gear and flaps, then turn 180° to E and descend [[23:193|IFH 7-32]].

takeaways: Same bank at a lower speed means a faster turn: shallow the bank as you slow, steepen it as you speed up.
Standard-rate bank is about 15 percent of true airspeed; the turn coordinator or turn rate indicator has the final word.
Throttle for speed, elevator for altitude, rudder for the ball, trim for the pressure.
Underpower or overpower for big changes, then set the new power before the target.
Manifold pressure is primary while the power is set and the speed is changing; near the new speed the airspeed indicator is primary again.
Partial panel: altimeter and VSI for pitch, turn coordinator for bank, compass only when steady.
Trim sets an airspeed: trim as you go, final trim once the speed is steady.
Teach level first, then the easier turning method, then the IFH patterns, then partial panel.
cfi_notes: Two rules of thumb for standard-rate bank disagree. IFH 7-19 uses 15 percent of TAS, about 13.5° at 90 knots [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]; IFH 4-11 says divide the airspeed by 10 and add 7, which gives 16° at 90 knots [[23:88|IFH 4-11]]. The PHAK formula gives about 14° at 90 knots TAS [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]]. Teach one rule as a starting point and the turn coordinator or turn rate indicator as the final check [[23:181|IFH 7-20]] [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].

IFH 7-24 and Figure 7-38 make the airspeed indicator primary for power as the speed nears the new value [[23:185|IFH 7-24]], but the next page says "pitch attitude becomes primary for power control" when approaching the desired airspeed [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. That sentence matches no other IFH primary list; teach the airspeed indicator, and be ready if an examiner quotes it.

IFH 5-19 says the attitude indicator's knob raises or lowers the miniature aircraft to compensate for pitch trim changes as the airspeed changes [[23:114|IFH 5-19]], while IFH 6-5 says set it in level flight at cruise and do not change it for other speeds, so it shows a true pitch picture [[23:138|IFH 6-5]]. The Chapter 7 examples follow 6-5: two-and-a-half bar widths nose-high at 100 knots with the gear down [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

The IFH says the bank for a given rate of turn is proportional to the true airspeed [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. Strictly, the PHAK formula makes the tangent of the bank proportional to TAS [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]]; at normal standard-rate banks of 10° to 20° [[23:214|IFH 7-53]] the difference is small, so the IFH wording is fine for teaching.

The IFH glass chapter has no section on changing airspeed in turns, and its example loses all attitude and heading with the AHRS, with no standby turn coordinator for the pilot [[23:217|IFH 7-56]] [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. Teach the round-dial procedure with the glass instruments, and the failure modes from the airplane's AFM supplement.

The PTS says its listed common errors may or may not be found in the Task references [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]]. The IFH lists for straight-and-level flight and turns [[23:174|IFH 7-13]] [[23:186|IFH 7-25]] [[23:187|IFH 7-26]] fit under the PTS headings, but "bank not varied with the speed" is this lesson's reading of IFH 4-11 and 7-24 [[23:88|IFH 4-11]] [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]; say so if asked.

The IFH Chapter 7 examples assume a single-engine airplane with retractable gear and flaps [[23:162|IFH 7-1]] and give manifold pressure settings [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]. In a fixed-pitch trainer the tachometer takes that role [[23:170|IFH 7-9]], and the underpower and target settings come from the POH and practice.

Expect the examiner to ask why the bank changes with speed, the primary instruments before, during and after the change, which turning method is easier, what the compass does in a partial panel slowdown, and to fly an error in a turn. The evaluator acts as a student and expects an explanation with no prompting [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]] [[FAA-S-8081-9E:15|PTS Unsatisfactory Performance]], and the IFH calls the turning speed change a test of all three basic skills [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].
gaps: No source gives the power settings, attitudes or underpower values for a particular trainer; the IFH uses a sample retractable airplane with 23, 18 and 15 inches [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]. Get them from the POH/AFM and flight practice.

The CFII PTS gives no tolerances for this Task. The speed tolerances in these sources are ATC's plus or minus 10 knots for assigned speeds [[33:283|AIM 4-4-12]] and the Instrument Rating ACS standard of airspeed ±10 knots, with altitude ±100 feet in level flight, selected headings ±10° and bank ±5° during turns [[FAA-S-ACS-8C:16|IR ACS IR.IV.A.S1]] (the Instrument lesson IR.IV.A lists them).
No source gives a separate partial panel procedure for changing airspeed in a turn; this lesson applies the IFH partial panel rules to the IFH speed-change procedure and marks that as Application.

No source says how far to underpower or overpower with a fixed-pitch propeller, or exactly how much to lead the new speed; the IFH says only that the lead depends on how fast the airplane responds [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].
No source says whether the turn rate indicator survives an AHRS or magnetometer failure in a given glass system; the IFH shows one example [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. Check the AFM supplement.

activities.title: Bank for the speed
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: IFH rule of thumb (15 percent of TAS): about what bank gives a standard-rate turn at 120 knots TAS?
Your student slows from 120 to 100 knots TAS in a standard-rate turn. By the same rule, by how many degrees should the bank come down?
items.why: 120 knots: about 18°. 100 knots: 10 + 5 = 15°. 18 - 15 = 3° less bank [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]; the IFH says to decrease the bank during a reduction of airspeed [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

items.q: She keeps 18° of bank at 100 knots TAS. Using the PHAK formula, rate = 1,091 × tan(bank) ÷ TAS, with tan 18° = 0.325, what is her rate of turn?
items.why: 1,091 × 0.325 ÷ 100 = about 3.5° per second [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]] [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]], faster than the 3° per second of standard rate [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

items.q: IFH chapter 4 gives another rule: airspeed ÷ 10, plus 7. What bank does it give at 90 knots?
items.why: 90 ÷ 10 = 9, plus 7 = 16° [[23:88|IFH 4-11]]. The 15 percent rule gives about 13.5° [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]; the turn coordinator is the final check [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

items.q: Each 180° turn in the racetrack pattern is flown at standard rate. How many seconds does each take?
items.why: Standard rate is 3° per second [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]: 180 ÷ 3 = 60 seconds [[23:191|IFH 7-30]].

activities.title: The IFH slowdown to 95 knots, gear and flaps down
activities.intro: Put the IFH steps in order, first to last, then tap Check.
steps: Maintain 2,500 rpm, since high power is used in the full drag configuration
Reduce manifold pressure to 10 inches and speed up the cross-check
Trim for the higher angle of attack and the lower torque
Lower the gear at 115 knots; raise the pitch and trim off some back pressure
At about 105 knots, smoothly set 18 inches
Lower the flaps while adding power to 25 inches; trim to hold altitude and heading
activities.why: IFH sequence for 120 to 95 knots with gear and flaps [[23:172|IFH 7-11]] [[23:173|IFH 7-12]], repeated for the glass panel [[23:203|IFH 7-42]].

activities.title: Pitch, bank, power, or rudder and trim?
activities.intro: Tap each picture, then the control that fixes it.

items.t: Altimeter creeping down as the speed decays
VSI showing a climb as the power comes in
Turn coordinator past the standard-rate mark as the airplane slows
Turn rate trend short of the standard-rate tick as the speed builds
Airspeed nearing the target with the throttle still at the underpower setting
Altitude on target, airspeed 10 knots low and still falling
Ball off center after a power change
Back pressure still being held after the speed has settled

activities.why: Pitch holds altitude as the speed changes [[23:172|IFH 7-11]] [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]; the bank varies with airspeed to keep the rate [[23:185|IFH 7-24]] [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]; lead the airspeed with the new power, and with altitude on target the power is the fix [[23:174|IFH 7-13]] [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]; rudder centers the ball and trim removes held pressure [[23:173|IFH 7-12]] [[23:204|IFH 7-43]].

activities.title: True or false: speed-change myths
activities.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

cards.s: An airplane is trimmed for an airspeed, so every intentional speed change needs a retrim.
cards.why: True. Trim is a function of speed [[23:85|IFH 4-8]], and any time the airspeed changes, retrimming is required [[23:204|IFH 7-43]].

cards.s: Underpowering is needed for every speed change, even a 5-knot one.
cards.why: False. For small changes, or airplanes that slow down or speed up quickly, it is not necessary [[23:170|IFH 7-9]].

cards.s: Holding the same bank while slowing keeps the turn at standard rate.
cards.why: False. If the speed decreases without a change in bank, the rate of turn increases [[23:88|IFH 4-11]].

cards.s: A quick throttle reduction in IMC can lead a disoriented pilot to pull into a nose-up or stall attitude.
cards.why: True. That is the deceleration side of the somatogravic illusion [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

cards.s: An analog attitude indicator may show a slight nose-up error during a rapid acceleration.
cards.why: True, and a nose-down error in a rapid deceleration; the errors are small and correct themselves within a minute or so [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].

cards.s: On a north heading, a partial panel slowdown makes the compass show a turn.
cards.why: False. On north or south headings, changing airspeed causes no compass error; on east or west headings, deceleration shows a south turn [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

activities.title: A turning slowdown, one call at a time
activities.intro: Your instrument student flies a retractable single like the IFH example: 23 inches for 120 knots, 18 inches for 100 knots. It is VMC and you are the safety pilot.

steps.s: Before the flight she asks how to change speed in a turn. Which method do you introduce first?
options: Establish the turn, then change the speed
Start the slowdown and the roll-in together
Slow down first, then roll into the turn
Let the bank float and fix the rate later
steps.why: Changing speed after the turn is established is the easier method [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]; simple to complex [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

steps.s: Established at standard rate, she pulls the power to 15 inches. As the speed decays, the turn coordinator moves past the mark.
options: Hold the bank; the rate will settle
Shallow the bank and raise the pitch
Add rudder against the turn
Add power back to 23 inches
steps.why: During a reduction of airspeed, decrease the bank and increase the pitch to hold altitude and standard rate [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. Rudder against the turn would make it uncoordinated [[23:89|IFH 4-12]].

steps.s: Now she is staring at the manifold pressure gauge and is 60 feet high.
options: Tell her to trim nose-down right away
Take the controls and demonstrate again
Point out the fixation and get her scanning
Have her add power to stop the climb
steps.why: Gazing at the power instrument during an airspeed change is a common fixation, and a small power error matters less than large altitude and heading errors [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]. Safety permitting, let her find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

steps.s: Reaching 100 knots, she leaves the throttle at 15 inches and the speed falls to 94.
options: Failure to lead the airspeed: set 18 inches sooner
Normal: every speed change overshoots a little
A trim error: she needed nose-down trim
A bank error: the turn bled off the speed
steps.why: Adjust the throttle before the airspeed reaches the target, or the airplane slows below it [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]; set about 18 inches as the speed nears 100 knots [[23:172|IFH 7-11]] [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

steps.s: You cover the gyros. On a heading of 270 she slows and the compass swings toward south.
options: Bank to stop the apparent turn
Hold the wings level; read the compass once steady
Uncover the heading indicator
Use the compass as the primary bank instrument
steps.why: Deceleration on an east or west heading gives a south-turn indication [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]; read the compass only in straight, unaccelerated flight [[23:187|IFH 7-26]] and keep the turn coordinator level with the ball centered [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].

steps.s: Back on the ground, how do you start the debrief?
options: Give her your grade first
List every error you saw
Skip it if the flight went well
Ask for her self-assessment first
steps.why: Collaborative assessment starts with the learner's self-assessment, followed by a discussion that compares it with the instructor's [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].
